Abstract Background  Community-based chest X-ray (CXR) screening has been widely performed to improve tuberculosis identification in elderly populations, but comparative evidence against mode of symptom-driven case finding remains scarce. Methods  We conducted three annual rounds of mass CXR screening among individuals aged over 60 years in Lanxi City, China, from 2021 to 2023. Tuberculosis cases identified through CXR screening were compared with concurrent, symptom-driven case presentations via routine surveillance. Restricted cubic spline and multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to examine factors associated with distinct detection pathways. Results  At the individual level, a total of 831 tuberculosis cases were identified through two modes. CXR mass screening detected more patients with less typical symptoms, while symptom-driven detection was more effective in females (aOR = 0.59, 95% CI 0.39–0.88), bacteriologically confirmed cases (aOR = 0.42, 95% CI 0.27–0.63), and those aged greater than 80 (aOR = 0.50, 95% CI 0.30–0.82). Age showed a nonlinear association with mass screening yield, with peak effectiveness between 60 and 66 years while no significance was found for BMI. In population-level analysis, CXR mass screening outperformed symptom-driven detection for case identification in the first round but declined and reversed by the third round. Subgroup analyses revealed potential benefits among individuals with diabetes or prior tuberculosis history, particularly within two years post-diagnosis or treatment. Conclusions  Community-based CXR screening could effectively detect incremental tuberculosis cases with atypical or mild symptoms. The young-old would benefit from mass CXR screening, while more accessible services were needed for the very elderly. Elderly individuals with diabetes or prior tuberculosis history should be prioritized, with intensified monitoring within two years after diagnosis or treatment completion.

​Introduction As a chronic infectious disease, tuberculosis causes huge challenges in low- and middle-income countries glob­ ally, especially among the 30 high burden countries [1]. According to the latest report released by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2025, there were 10.7 million new tuberculosis cases globally, with an esti­ mated incidence rate of 131 per 100,000 population [2]. In recent years, with the enhancement of global surveil­ lance capacity and improvements in diagnostic technolo­ gies, the gap in undetected tuberculosis cases has been gradually narrowing. However, a disparity of approxi­ mately 2.7 million persists between estimated data and reported results [3]. To address this gap, active screening interventions, particularly community-based active case finding have been implemented to improve case detec­ tion in populations with limited healthcare access and well-confined regions [4].

Globally, passive case detection (PCF), where patients seek care based on their symptoms, remains the domi­ nant tuberculosis detection strategy [5, 6]. Recent studies showed that a clinically significant proportion of active pulmonary tuberculosis cases, particularly among elderly populations, presented with nonspecific or asymptomatic manifestations, substantially compromising the sensitiv­ ity of conventional PCF approaches [7, 8]. In this con­ text, mass screening such as using chest radiography has gained prominence as a viable case-finding modality in resource-constrained settings, owing to its optimal bal­ ance between diagnostic sensitivity and specificity for case identification [9–11].

Since 2021, we have conducted three annual rounds of active pulmonary tuberculosis case detection using Chest X-ray (CXR) screening among elderly populations in Lanxi City, China. This study aims to evaluate the dif­ ference between community-based CXR screening and concurrent symptom-driven group at both the individual and population levels. It would help identify effective patient demographic profiles of CXR screening for fur­ ther optimal screening intervention and clarify key target populations for screening in elderly communities as well.

Study design A previous study described the similar study design of the first round of CXR screening in community [13]. The screening period for each round was one year, tar­ geting local elderly individuals aged 60 and above. Each round of mass screening covered two stages: preliminary community mobilization and CXR screening in local community health centers. CXR screening underwent two rounds of review by community-based radiologists and peers from higher-level institutions. Presumptive tuberculosis cases were referred to designated hospitals for further evaluation. We defined tuberculosis cases identified through community-based CXR screening as presumptive tuberculosis cases detected through CXR screening in local community and confirmed via refer­ ral within three months after this specific mass screen­ ing. Symptom-driven tuberculosis cases in this study referred to pulmonary tuberculosis patients aged 60 or above who were notified in Lanxi City from 2021 to 2023 after seeking care at designated hospitals due to tuber­ culosis-related symptoms. Information on these patients was first obtained from the tuberculosis-specific report­ ing data in the China Disease Control and Prevention Information System and subsequently verified through field checks at designated hospitals to confirm symptom- driven Tuberculosis cases. Two scenarios were excluded: (1) tuberculosis cases who did not participate in commu­ nity-based active screening but were identified through routine physical examinations at local general hospitals and subsequently referred. (2) tuberculosis cases who were diagnosed during medical examinations or hospi­ talization for other diseases. For both community-based mass screening and symptom-driven tuberculosis cases identification, field verification at designated hospi­ tals was conducted to ultimately confirm diagnosis and patient-reported information, while relevant variables were collected. All diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis cases received standardized treatment regimens, and their closed contacts received comprehensive interven­ tions in accordance with national guidelines.

Besides, the annual surveillance data for individu­ als with prior tuberculosis were constructed based on the time interval between treatment completion or cure

Study definitions In this study, we classified patient detection methods into two categories: community-based CXR screening and symptom-based case presentation. The former referred to cases identified through systematic community-based CXR screening of presumptive individuals, followed by referral and diagnostic confirmation. Symptom-based case presentation was defined as tuberculosis cases detected when patients proactively sought medical care due to TB-related symptoms. The definition of bacteriologically confirmed and clinically diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis cases in both groups referred to the Diagnostic Criteria for Pulmonary Tuberculosis (WS 288–2017) in China [14]. Smoking statuses were catego­ rized into 3 groups as nonsmoker, former smoker, and current smoker. Former smokers were defined as people with a previous history of smoking but now quit; cur­ rent smokers were defined as people who consumed any tobacco product within the past 30 days and had a life­ time cigarette use of 100 or more. Alcohol use was also categorized into 3 subgroups as nondrinkers, occasional drinkers who drink less than twice a week, and frequent drinkers who drink at least twice a week [12]. Population differences in tuberculosis case detection between community-based CXR screening and symptom- driven group At the population level, we compared the yield of tuber­ culosis detection between serial CXR screenings and concurrent symptom-driven presentations. In the first round, the CXR screening identified significantly more active pulmonary tuberculosis than the symptom-driven group with risk ratio (RR) 1.63 and its 95% CI 1.28 to

2.07. By the second round, no significant difference was observed between the two models. Analysis of surveillance data for populations with prior tuberculosis or diabetes We further examined the surveillance data on prior tuberculosis group and diabetes group. Among elderly patients in Lanxi City who completed the tuberculosis treatment course and were cured between 2014 and 2020, 47 cases developed tuberculosis again within the follow­ ing five years. Notably, 65.96% (31/47) of these recur­ rence cases occurred within two years after completing the treatment. Additionally, among elderly patients diag­ nosed with diabetes, 121 developed tuberculosis within five years of their diabetes diagnosis. Of these, 65.29% (79/121) occurred within the first two years after diabetes diagnosis. It was shown in Fig. 4.

Discussion In this study, we compared case detection via commu­ nity CXR screening with those found through symp­ tom-driven presentations. RCS analysis clarified the key individual attributes in improving the effectiveness of CXR screening among the elderly. Meanwhile, our find­ ings revealed significant differences in the demographic characteristics and clinical manifestations of tuber­ culosis identified by both strategies, providing a more detailed profile of targeted objectives by CXR screening. Finally, from a population perspective along with histori­ cal surveillance data, our findings indicated that active

screening should be prioritized or intensified for individ­ uals within two years following completion of tuberculo­ sis treatment or cure, as well as for those within two years after a diabetes diagnosis. Our findings offer important data support and decision-making basis for optimizing tuberculosis control strategies in the elderly population, particularly for implementing targeted screening in high- risk subgroups.

RCS analysis revealed a significant non-linear relation­ ship between age and case finding in different modes. Between the ages of 60 and 66, the odds ratio of patients in active cases findings increased rapidly, indicating that the relative yield of CXR screening improved with age during this interval. Some reasons might explain this result. Within this age interval, they maintained a cer­ tain level of social mobility and possessed discretionary time after retirement, resulting in higher accessibility to community-based screening [18]; meanwhile, the clinical symptoms of tuberculosis in the old population tended to be more insidious or atypical [19–21]. CXR screen­ ing could increase the chance of detecting more “hid­ den cases” and simultaneously raise the possibility of detecting more asymptomatic or atypical tuberculosis cases [7, 12]. This makes it a critical window for achiev­ ing early tuberculosis control. Consequently, invest­ ing community-based CXR screening resources in this group yielded incremental marginal returns with each additional year of age. After the age of 75, the odds ratio gradually declined, implying that case findings from community-based CXR screening diminished in the older population. This shift may be explained by some

Fig. 3  Tuberculosis prevalence to case notification ratio among distinct subgroup of elderly groups. It was stratified by sex, age group (60–69, 70–80, ≥80 years), diagnosed diabetes, and prior tuberculosis diagnosis, shown across three years

Page 8 of 11 Liu et al. BMC Geriatrics         (2026) 26:1202

reasons below. Firstly, the accessibility of community- based CXR screening declined with age. Older adults faced physical functional decline and mobility challenges, making it difficult to participate in centralized commu­ nity screening [7]; secondly, their frequent medical visits due to multiple comorbidities increased the likelihood of tuberculosis detection during routine care, thereby par­ tially offsetting the relative benefits of mass screening [22, 23]. This indicated that for individuals aged 75 and above, CXR screening strategies in community required corresponding adjustments. That is to say, sole reliance on centralized CXR screening for tuberculosis in this specific age group may face limited yield, and alternative approaches such as door-to-door screening and integra­ tion into multi-chronic disease co-management should be explored to improve tuberculosis detection among the elderly population [24–27].

A notable negative finding in our study among the elderly subgroup was that BMI was not a predictor of the suitable pathway through which tuberculosis cases should be detected. From the perspective of optimizing resource allocation, prioritizing case finding strategies

based on BMI may be inefficient in the elderly popula­ tion. Whether driven by symptom‑based healthcare- seeking or active participation in mass screening, the decision‑making process among older adults was likely influenced more by factors such as symptom percep­ tion, functional status, and socioeconomic determinants, rather than anthropometric indices alone [28, 29]. In future, greater emphasis should be placed on the relative importance of refined age stratification and comorbid­ ity management in guiding targeted screening. Concur­ rently, we should explore efficient indicators, particularly behavioral and social determinants, to better differentiate the pathways of patient identification.

Third, multivariate analysis further identified impor­ tant independent factors influencing the pathways through which patients were detected. Older age group (greater than 80 years), female gender, bacteriologically confirmed positivity, and the presence of typical symp­ toms such as cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, fever, and appetite loss all significantly increased the likelihood of patients being detected through the symptom-driven pathway. These findings align with clinical observations

At the population level, stratified annual comparisons across different subgroups revealed dynamic variations in the effectiveness of screening strategies. Overall, the detection rate of the first round of community-based CXR screening was significantly higher than that of symptom-driven detection. However, as the number of screening rounds increased, its effectiveness gradu­ ally declined and reversed by the third round. This may reflect the substantial “depletion” of the pool of tuber­ culosis cases among individuals inclined to participate in mass screening after multiple rounds caused by self- selection bias [36]. Additionally, the possible decline in tuberculosis cases within the age groups, changes in pop­ ulation structure, and the potential impact of screening during the COVID-19 period may all have played a role. Notably, the benefits of CXR mass screening existed in some specific subgroups such as individuals with diabe­ tes and individuals with prior tuberculosis. Regarding the latter, CXR mass screening demonstrated higher detec­ tion rates than symptom-driven group starting from the second round. These findings are further validated by local surveillance data. About 65% of TB recurrences in cured patients and new TB cases among diabetic patients happened in the first two years after treatment or diag­ nosis. Thus, both high-risk groups should intensify more comprehensive interventions such as regularly collect­ ing sputum samples and concentratedly implementing tongue swab screening [37, 38]. It could facilitate early detection and treatment of recurrent or new tuberculo­ sis cases, thereby curbing transmission and improving patient prognosis.

Some limitations should be mentioned. Firstly, the symptoms reported in some patients’ chief complaint during their initial registration in designated hospitals may be inconsistent with those reported during the mass screening, potentially due to participants' stigma at the screening site or improper questioning techniques by community healthcare workers. Although we adjusted it based on chief complaints, potential bias may still exist. Secondly, due to the insidious onset of diabetes, we used the date of the patient’s first diabetes diagnosis in the monitoring data, which may have some impact on the subsequent duration of tuberculosis onset.

In conclusion, within the context of a high-burden city in Eastern China, a community-based CXR screen­ ing can effectively identify tuberculosis cases with mild or asymptomatic status compared with symptom-driven case detection at the individual level. Meanwhile, the current mass screening protocol should be maintained for the younger elderly group to improve case detection, while more convenient and precise services should be developed for the very elderly population. At the popu­ lation level, elderly individuals with diabetes or a history of tuberculosis should be prioritized as core screening populations, with an intensified monitoring mecha­ nism established within two years post-treatment or post-diagnosis.
